title: Song of Solomon 7:1–9
context: In a poem the WEB assigns to the Lover, he praises the Beloved from her feet to her head in images drawn from art, nature, and the land, from Heshbon and Lebanon to Carmel, ending with the wish that her words be like the best wine. Readers in both traditions take the poem as delight in a beloved spouse and honor within covenant love, and many in both traditions also read the Song as a picture of God and Israel or of Christ and the church. Versification: English/WEB 7:1–13 is Hebrew 7:2–14, and WEB 6:13 is Hebrew 7:1; this page keeps the WEB numbers. Speaker names (Lover, Beloved, Friends, Brothers) follow the WEB headings, which are interpretive and are not part of the Hebrew text.

verses.text: How beautiful are your feet in sandals, prince’s daughter! Your rounded thighs are like jewels, the work of the hands of a skillful workman.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lover begins, “How beautiful are your feet in sandals, prince’s daughter!” Arminian readers who read the Song literally see a husband honoring his bride with dignity, calling her a “prince’s daughter.”

The images are poetic and should be read with restraint, as delight rather than display.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the honor in the title “prince’s daughter,” and some read it allegorically of the church made noble by Christ (cf. Ps 45:13).

Shared ground: Readers in both traditions hold literal and allegorical readings side by side. The praise expresses delight and respect within covenant love.

verses.text: Your body is like a round goblet, no mixed wine is wanting. Your waist is like a heap of wheat, set about with lilies.
verses.arminianNotes:
The praise continues with images of a goblet and a heap of wheat “set about with lilies.” Arminian readers note that the pictures come from feasting and harvest, suggesting abundance and blessing.

The poem’s purpose is admiration, not description for its own sake.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see images of plenty and provision. Those who read the Song allegorically have seen in such pictures the fruitfulness God gives his people.

Shared ground: both traditions read these lines briefly and with restraint, as praise within faithful love.

verses.text: Your two breasts are like two fawns, that are twins of a roe.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lover repeats an image of twin fawns, used earlier in the Song (cf. 4:5). Arminian readers note that the repetition marks continuity in his delight.

The gentle animal imagery suggests tenderness rather than possession.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the repeated image as a sign of steady affection.

Shared ground: both traditions treat the line with restraint, reading it as poetry of tenderness within covenant love, whether taken literally or as a figure of God’s love for his people.

verses.text: Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon by the gate of Bathrabbim. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon which looks toward Damascus.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon by the gate of Bathrabbim.” Arminian readers note the use of place names to convey beauty and stillness.

Heshbon was a city east of the Jordan (Num 21:25–26); the gate of Bathrabbim and “the tower of Lebanon” are not identified with certainty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see images of strength and dignity in the ivory tower and the tower looking toward Damascus.

Shared ground: both traditions hedge the geography and read the images as praise of beauty joined with honor.

verses.text: Your head on you is like Carmel. The hair of your head like purple. The king is held captive in its tresses.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Your head on you is like Carmel... The king is held captive in its tresses.” Arminian readers note the playful image of a king held captive by love.

Carmel is usually taken as the mountain known for its beauty, though the exact point of the comparison is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see love’s power over even a king. Those who read allegorically have connected the “king” with God or Christ delighting in his people, as a reading.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as admiration and devotion, not as a theological contrast.

verses.text: How beautiful and how pleasant you are, love, for delights!
verses.arminianNotes:
“How beautiful and how pleasant you are, love, for delights!” Arminian readers note that the Lover now speaks of her as a whole person.

The line sums up his delight in her.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a summary of joyful admiration.

Shared ground: both traditions see delight within covenant love as a good gift of God, and allegorical readers in both traditions hear an echo of God’s delight in his people (cf. Isa 62:4–5).

verses.text: This, your stature, is like a palm tree, your breasts like its fruit.
verses.arminianNotes:
“This, your stature, is like a palm tree.” Arminian readers note the image of uprightness and grace.

The palm suggests dignity and fruitfulness in a dry land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see beauty and strength in the palm tree image.

Shared ground: both traditions read the comparison briefly and with restraint, as praise within marriage or as a figure of the beauty God gives his people.

verses.text: I said, “I will climb up into the palm tree. I will take hold of its fruit.” Let your breasts be like clusters of the vine, the smell of your breath like apples.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lover says, “I will climb up into the palm tree,” and wishes that her breath be fragrant “like apples.” Arminian readers note his longing to draw near to the one he loves.

The imagery is poetic and should not be pressed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see desire expressed within the poem’s covenant setting.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with restraint, seeing longing for closeness as part of faithful love, and allegorical readers see the soul’s longing for communion with God.

verses.text: Your mouth is like the best wine, that goes down smoothly for my beloved, gliding through the lips of those who are asleep.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Your mouth is like the best wine, that goes down smoothly for my beloved.” Arminian readers note the image of wine for joy and delight (cf. 1:2).

The WEB assigns the whole verse to the Lover; some readers hear the Beloved answering in its second half.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see words of joy and refreshment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the closing line of the poem as delight in shared love, and they hedge the change of speaker.
